stem: For which two workloads is session mode the most appropriate execution mode? (Select two.)

options.text: Fifty independent circuits, all known upfront, that you want to push through the queue as cheaply as possible in one go.
An experiment that needs the QPU reserved exclusively so that no other users' jobs or calibrations interleave with your circuits.
A variational eigensolver whose next circuit depends on the classical optimizer's use of the previous result.
A single circuit you want to run once as quickly as possible.
A large collection of unrelated benchmarking circuits, where minimizing cost usually matters more than latency.
A hundred-point parameter sweep of one circuit, where the whole sweep is usually submitted as a single primitive job anyway.

explanation.correct: Sessions shine for iterative workloads whose next input is not ready at the outset, such as a variational loop that waits on the classical optimizer, and for experiments that need dedicated, exclusive access to the QPU, with no other users' jobs or calibration jobs during the active window. Both justify a session's higher cost; independent work known upfront belongs in batch, and a single request in job mode.

distractors.A: Independent circuits known upfront that you want to run cheaply are the classic case for batch mode, which is generally less expensive than a session.
distractors.D: A single circuit run should use job mode; a session gives no queuing benefit for the first (only) job and costs more.
distractors.E: Cost-sensitive, independent benchmarking circuits belong in batch mode, not in a more expensive session.
distractors.F: A parameter sweep is one PUB with an array of parameter values, so it is already a single job — there is no iteration for a session to accelerate and nothing gained from dedicated access.
